claims.claim: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries; the arteries carry blood from the heart to other parts of the body.

Systolic pressure is the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats and pumps blood (the top/first number, the highest point); diastolic pressure is the pressure between beats when the heart rests (the bottom/second number). A reading written 120/80 means a systolic of 120 and a diastolic of 80.

For adults, a normal blood pressure level is less than 120/80 mmHg — the AHA category table lists NORMAL as less than 120 systolic AND less than 80 diastolic, and the CDC states a normal blood pressure level is less than 120/80 mmHg.

Blood pressure categories come from guidelines, not verdicts: the thresholds used to diagnose high blood pressure have changed over time — some clinicians use 140/90 mmHg (a 2003 guideline) and others use 130/80 mmHg (a 2017 guideline); blood pressure changes through the day based on activities, and a diagnosis follows blood pressure that stays consistently above normal.

Blood pressure is measured with a blood pressure cuff: providers use a gauge, a stethoscope or electronic sensor, and a blood pressure cuff around the arm, and they take two or more readings at separate appointments before making a diagnosis.

Factors the CDC links to higher blood pressure: eating too much sodium (an element in table salt) increases blood pressure; not getting enough regular physical activity; having obesity or overweight means the heart must work harder to pump blood; high blood pressure can run in a family and genes likely play a role; managing stress is among the CDC/NHLBI lifestyle steps for blood pressure control.
High blood pressure usually has no warning signs or symptoms, and many people do not know they have it; measuring blood pressure is the only way to know whether a person has high blood pressure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The threshold used to diagnose high blood pressure differs between guidelines
positions: Some clinicians diagnose high blood pressure at 140/90 mmHg or higher, based on the 2003 JNC7 guideline
Other clinicians diagnose at 130/80 mmHg or higher, based on the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline
The NORMAL reference (<120/<80 mmHg) is consistent across CDC, AHA, MedlinePlus, and NHLBI
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the normal adult reference (<120/<80 mmHg) with attribution, and honestly notes that the diagnostic lines come from guidelines that have shifted over the years (140/90 vs 130/80 per the CDC) — categories are guideline-based, not verdicts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether stress is a cause of high blood pressure
positions: CDC and NHLBI list reducing/managing stress among the lifestyle steps that help control blood pressure
Stress is understood to push blood pressure up in the moment, while its long-term role as a driver of chronic hypertension is less settled
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states factually that stress can push a reading up and that managing stress is among the steps the CDC and NHLBI list for blood pressure control — it does not claim stress alone causes chronic hypertension.

positions: A single reading can be affected by activity, stress, or the moment (e.g., a rushed morning)
Diagnosis requires blood pressure that stays consistently above normal, checked on two or more readings at separate appointments
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches that a single reading is not a diagnosis: providers take two or more readings at separate appointments before making a call (MedlinePlus), and blood pressure changes through the day based on activities (CDC).

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-4 generated draft contained no factual clinical content — it was generic boilerplate ('Blood Pressure is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations') with no definition, no numbers, and no evidence, so nothing in it survived the rewrite.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generic draft with a source-verified lesson: working definition attributed to CDC and MedlinePlus; systolic/diastolic explained per MedlinePlus/CDC; normal reference <120/<80 mmHg per CDC and AHA; measurement description per MedlinePlus; risk factors per CDC; the 'usually silent' claim per CDC and MedlinePlus; honest guideline note per CDC.
